title: Where's the post office? — asking the way
goal: Ask the way and understand the answer — while setting up the locative, the place form, and seeing why one and the same preposition can mean "to" or "in/at" depending on the noun's ending.
bekal: ask the way and follow directions given by a stranger in the street
form the locative and recognize the sound changes *k → c*, *g → z*, *h → s*
choose between the accusative (where to) and the locative (where) after *u* and *na*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Gdje je pošta?
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost among the little lanes of Stari Grad. He stops an old man walking slowly with a bag of bread.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, where's the post office?

lines.speaker: Prolaznik:
lines.text: Pošta? Idite pravo, pa prvo lijevo.
lines.id: The post office? Go straight, then take the first left.
lines.literal: post-office? go-pl straight, then first left.

lines.speaker: Prolaznik:
lines.text: Nije, pet minuta pješke. Pored banke, preko puta džamije.
lines.id: No, five minutes on foot. Next to the bank, across from the mosque.
lines.literal: not-it-is, five minutes-gen-pl on-foot. next-to bank-gen, across road-gen mosque-gen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A ima li tu negdje i bankomat?
lines.id: Is there an ATM there too?
lines.literal: and there-is whether there somewhere also ATM?

lines.speaker: Prolaznik:
lines.text: Ima, na uglu. U pošti možete platiti i račune.
lines.id: There is, on the corner. You can also pay bills at the post office.
lines.literal: there-is, on corner-loc. in post-office-loc you(pl)-can pay also bills-acc-pl.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hvala vam! A gdje je najbliža apoteka?
lines.id: Thank you! And where's the nearest pharmacy?
lines.literal: thanks to-you(pl)! and where it-is nearest-f pharmacy?

lines.speaker: Prolaznik:
lines.text: Apoteka je na trgu, blizu tramvajske stanice.
lines.id: The pharmacy is on the square, near the tram stop.
lines.literal: pharmacy it-is on square-loc, near tram-f-gen stop-gen.

lines.speaker: Prolaznik:
lines.text: Jeste! Baščaršija je iza vas. Samo se okrenite.
lines.id: You are! Baščaršija is behind you. Just turn around.
lines.literal: you-are! Baščaršija it-is behind you(pl)-gen. only self turn-pl.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Ah! Thank you. I got lost.

lines.speaker: Prolaznik:
lines.text: Nema problema, sine. Svi se izgube u Sarajevu prvi put.
lines.id: No problem, son. Everyone gets lost in Sarajevo the first time.
lines.literal: there's-no problem-gen, son-voc. all self they-lose in Sarajevo-loc first time.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thanks once again. Have a nice day!

notes: **Count the *-u* and *-i* endings in this dialogue: *na uglu, u pošti, na trgu, u Sarajevu*.** That's the locative — the form a noun takes when it is a **place**. It never appears alone; there's always a preposition in front.

***Pored banke*, *preko puta džamije*, *blizu stanice* — all genitive.** Position words like *pored* (next to), *blizu* (near), *iza* (behind), *ispred* (in front of), *preko puta* (across from) take the genitive you set up in unit 8. So two cases work side by side in this dialogue: the genitive for relative position, the locative after *u* and *na*.

***Idite pravo* and *okrenite se* are commands.** The polite form ends in *-ite* or *-te*; the casual form drops that ending: *idi pravo*, *okreni se*. You don't need to build them yourself at A1 — what you need is to **recognize them when someone gives you directions**, and the list below is enough for that.

***Izgubio sam se* — the past tense, set up fully in unit 14.** The formula is *sam* + a form ending in *-o* for a man, *-la* for a woman: *izgubio sam se* (man), *izgubila sam se* (woman). Learn these two forms whole now; it's a sentence you'll need before you get to unit 14.

***Sine!* — "son!"** From *sin* (son), in the vocative form. In Bosnia older people call younger ones this, and it's a sign of warmth, not rudeness. Its siblings: *kćeri* or *ćerko* (to a young woman), *brate* ("bro", to a male friend your age), *dušo* ("darling", used far more loosely than in English).

grammars.title: Lokativ — the place form
body: The third case, and it has one feature that makes it easy to spot: **it never stands without a preposition**. If you see *u*, *na*, or *o*, and the meaning isn't movement, what follows is certainly the locative.
after: **Good news worth printing in large type: the locative and the dative have exactly the same forms.** One ending, two jobs. When unit 13 sets up the dative, you won't learn a single new form — just a new job for a form you already know.

**Feminine words ending in *-ka, -ga, -ha* change that letter before *-i*.** *Banka → u banci*, *ruka → u ruci*, *Amerika → u Americi*, *knjiga → u knjizi*, *noga → na nozi*. The pattern: **k → c, g → z, h → s**. It sounds like extra complication, but it runs through all Slavic languages and you'll meet it again in unit 13 — learn three examples and the rest follows by itself.

**In the plural, one ending covers three jobs.** *-ima* (masculine & neuter) and *-ama* (feminine) are used for the **dative, locative, and instrumental** at once: *u gradovima* (in the cities), *prema gradovima* (toward the cities), *s gradovima* (with the cities). Three cases, one ending.

**Only five prepositions call for the locative:** *u* (in), *na* (on, at), *o* (about), *po* (around, all over; according to), *pri* (at, near — rare at A1). The most common: *u* and *na*, and *o* for "about" — *Govorimo o Sarajevu*, *Šta misliš o tome?*

grammars.title: U or na — and "to" versus "in/at"
body: This is the part that really separates fluent beginners from stumbling ones, and luckily it boils down to one idea: **the preposition stays the same, the case changes**.

head: Where to — accusative
Where — locative
Meaning
rows: to the post office / at the post office
to the square / on the square

after: **One preposition, two meanings.** *U grad* = heading into town; *u gradu* = being in town. English uses two words for this ("into" and "in"); Bosnian uses two endings. Once you see the pattern, it holds across the whole language without exception — and a mistake here is the one native speakers notice fastest.

**When *u*, when *na*?** Rough rule: *u* for spaces you can go into (*grad, kuća, soba, škola, pošta, prodavnica, restoran*), *na* for open surfaces and for activities (*trg, ulica, stanica, pijaca, more, planina, koncert, čas, posao, fakultet*).

**But don't push the logic too far.** Why *u školi* but *na fakultetu*? Why *u gradu* but *na selu*? There's no reason — just as English says *at school* but *in college*, *on the bus* but *in the car*. These pairs have to be learned like vocabulary. The ones you'll need most: *na poslu, na pijaci, na stanici, na ulici, na trgu, na fakultetu, na moru, na planini* — and almost everything else is *u*.
**Two frozen forms worth learning today:** *idem kući* (I'm going home) and *kod kuće sam* (I'm at home). Neither follows any pattern, and you'll use both every day.

blocks.text: An opener that always works: *Izvinite, gdje je…?* After that, all you need is the ability to **recognize** the answer — and the answer is almost always built from the words in this table.

head: Directions
Say it
English
rows: Behind / in front of the building.
Between the post office and the bank.
Is it far? — No, it's close.

blocks.title: Sarajevo on foot
items: The city stretches along a narrow valley between two ranges of hills, so you can hardly get truly lost: the *Miljacka* river runs from east to west, and the whole old town lies along it. If in doubt, find the river.

Sarajevo's tram is one of the oldest in Europe — its first line opened in 1885, before Vienna's. Tickets are bought at a kiosk (*kiosk*) or from the driver, and you validate them yourself as soon as you board. The sentence you need: *Jednu kartu, molim.*

In conversation, street names in Bosnia are almost always used without the word *ulica*: people say *Živim u Ferhadiji*, not *u ulici Ferhadija*. And in addresses the number comes **after** the street name — the opposite of the English habit.
